model.vision: A platform that produces predictably-engineered software and delivers and operates it on the customer's behalf.

objectives.statement: Predictable delivery: customers receive a duration, cost, and risk estimate before any code is written, and the delivered system arrives within the bounds of the chosen option.

Reliable design system: the platform provides an opinionated software design system that reliably produces maintainable applications — customers receive software engineered to a consistently verifiable standard regardless of who or what wrote it, a guarantee open-ended approaches to building software cannot make — making it the best and most efficient way to build complex applications.

Operations-first revenue with room to grow: the platform's initial commercial focus is a usage-based fee for operating delivered systems on the customer's behalf, while keeping the door open to charging for other value it creates — design and construction work, tokens, or consulting — as the business develops.

Customer self-sufficiency: the customer walks through the delivery process themselves but does not need engineering staff — the platform's AI agents play every technical delivery role (architect, senior developer, junior developer, tester, operator) while the customer remains the architect-of-record and requirements source.

Cost transparency at decision time: whenever the customer is asked to commit money, the projected operating cost is presented as a traceable, per-option figure, so every financial decision is informed by a forecast of what running the system will cost.

Extensibility to new categories of work: the platform can absorb new kinds of work products and new kinds of agents without re-architecting; the platform's delivery process remains stable as the infrastructure beneath it changes.
Audit and intervention: a human can take over, replay, or override any in-flight project; nothing the platform does is opaque or unrecoverable.

Programmatic extensibility: customers and their own tools and agents can drive the platform and stay in sync with its project state programmatically, with the same capabilities as a person using the app — integrating the platform into the workflows and tools they already use.
Accessible to non-coders: anyone who can think in systems can design, build, run, and host an application on the platform — no coding skill or engineering staff required.

The hard parts are handled: the platform absorbs the genuinely hard operational work — running systems in production, scaling, load and cost projection — so the customer never has to become an operations engineer.

Streamlined, opinionated delivery with configurable oversight: the delivery workflow is designed by the platform; how much human review it requires is configured per customer — from fully automatic to human approval at every chosen stage, with high-risk changes always human-reviewed.

model.mission: Carry each customer's idea through design, planning, construction, and operation as one guided, supervised workflow: the platform does the technical work through the agents it orchestrates and the tooling it generates, the customer stays in control through review, and the finished system is delivered — and, when the customer chooses, operated — on their behalf. The platform orchestrates; it does not hand-author code.

items.definition: The party that owns one or more projects and is billed by the platform for the services they use — today, hosting when the platform operates the delivered system.
The customer-side person who drives a project as architect-of-record — typically not an engineer — reviewing and approving the decisions their review policy routes to them.
A platform staff member with authority to intervene in a running project or operated system.
Any entity — an AI agent by default — that produces, reviews, or designs work products on behalf of a project.
A person who uses the customer's deployed application; they pay the customer, never the platform, and never interact with the platform.
A customer's undertaking to design, build, and optionally operate one software system, progressing through the system-design, project-design, and construction phases.
The durable record of a project's current phase, its design artifacts, and each artifact's review status.
A single work product of the delivery process belonging to a project — mission, glossary, architecture, plan, and so on — carrying a review status of awaiting, committed, rejected, or withdrawn.
A description of one business activity the customer's system must support, with its actors, trigger, and flow of steps.
A use case that captures the essence of the customer's business rather than a permutation of another; the small set the architecture must be validated against.
The computed duration, cost, and risk of one project option.
One candidate way to schedule and staff a project — such as normal, compressed, or subcritical — presented with its estimate for the customer's decision.
The software the platform built and now runs on the customer's behalf, consuming hosting capacity that the platform meters and bills.
The customer's choice of how far the platform's responsibility extends — building and delivering the system only, or also hosting and operating it.
The hosting and compute consumption an operated system accrues, metered by the platform and billed to the customer.
The customer's declared expectation of end-user load on the delivered application, used during project design to forecast operating cost.
The bounded time window over which a customer's metered usage is accumulated into a single service invoice.
The amount a customer owes the platform for one billing period's metered hosting usage, charged to their stored payment instrument.
The first project phase, in which the platform leads the Architect User from business vision to a validated, volatility-based architecture.
The second project phase, in which the platform turns the architecture into staffing-and-schedule options with estimated duration, cost, and risk.
The third project phase, in which Agents build, review, and integrate the system component by component against the chosen project option.
The ongoing phase after delivery, available by scenario choice, in which the platform hosts, scales, observes, and bills for the customer's system.
Capturing or refining a single design artifact together with the Architect User, whose review policy determines how it is approved at its review gate.
Forecasting what a system will cost to operate as a function of usage — at decision time from declared assumptions, and while running from observed load.
The decision point closing project design, where the customer chooses among the presented project options.
Assigning a discrete construction activity to an Agent and supervising it to completion or failure.
Evaluating a produced change against the project's design before it is accepted into the project.
Measuring construction progress against the plan at a regular cadence and triggering replanning when progress deviates significantly.
Placing a built system onto managed runtime capacity, or releasing that capacity when the system is withdrawn.
The platform's own decision to raise, lower, pause, or resume an operated system's capacity in response to observed demand, within the customer's chosen policy.
The autoscaling decision to hold an inactive operated system at zero capacity — and zero compute cost — while keeping it reachable for the next request.
Converting an operated system's observed consumption into billable usage attributed to its customer.
Pricing a customer's metered usage for a billing period and charging the resulting service invoice to their stored payment instrument.
Pausing, replaying, overriding, or taking over an in-flight project or operated system when it is stuck, unhealthy, or failing to pay.
The single per-project store holding everything the platform persists for that project — its state, its design artifacts, and its constructed outputs.
The system of record for a project's repository — where the project repository lives and its versions are kept; a hosted service or the customer's local machine.
The substrate that durably sequences and persists the platform's own long-running workflows — phase drives, billing cycles, and operation loops — across restarts and failures.
The external payment system through which the platform charges customers' stored instruments for its service invoices.

The customer's per-project choice of how much human approval the delivery workflow requires: fully automatic ('vibes'), human checkpoints at chosen stages ('checkpoints'), or human approval at every gate ('full'). Changes above a risk threshold always require human review, under any preset.
A point in the delivery workflow where a produced artifact or change waits for approval — by a human or automatically, per the project's review policy — before work continues.
A revision of an already-approved design artifact, driven by reviewer feedback or by changes to the artifacts it was based on; artifacts built on an amended basis are flagged for review.
The environment where a project's drafting and construction jobs execute — the customer's CI on their repository host, or their local machine — chosen per project as configuration.

items.statement: The platform must carry a customer through the production of a system without that customer assembling tools themselves.
The architect user must be able to co-author each design artifact with an automated assistant.
statedAs: The architect user must have a conversational surface for each Method artifact in which they can co-author with an automated assistant.

items.statement: The platform must enforce phase ordering and gate progression on artifact validity.
The platform must produce, for a planned project, multiple project options (normal, decompressed, compressed, subcritical), each with duration, cost, and risk.
statedAs: The platform must produce, for a planned system, multiple options (normal, decompressed, compressed, subcritical) with duration, cost, and risk.

items.statement: Cost estimation must be sensitive to which agents will perform which activities.
statedAs: Cost estimation must be sensitive to which workers will perform which activities.
The estimation engine must accept worker-model as an input parameter and emit an estimate per choice.

items.statement: Which kind of agent fulfills each delivery role (architect, senior, junior) must be allowed to vary.
statedAs: The construction hand-off model is policy: which kind of worker handles which Method role (architect / senior / junior).

items.statement: The platform must accept architect-user interaction over more than one entry channel.
statedAs: MCP is an entry-channel whose internal decomposition is a Client-layer choice, not an architectural pillar; read/write split is an internal MCP-server concern, not a system-level component.

items.statement: The platform must deploy and operate delivered systems on the customer's behalf.
statedAs: The platform must deploy and operate delivered systems on managed runtime, executing build and deploy through orchestrated workflows.

items.statement: The platform must produce, for a completed project, everything needed to deploy and operate the delivered system without manual handoff.
statedAs: The platform must produce, for a completed project, an artifact bundle deployable to managed runtime without manual handoff.

items.statement: The platform must serve heterogeneous and growing customer types without baking assumptions about customer size, internal team, or sophistication into its design.
statedAs: Customer types are heterogeneous and will grow; the platform must not bake assumptions about customer size, internal team, or sophistication into the architecture.

items.statement: The platform must bill customers under evolving commercial terms — initially a usage-based fee for hosting and operating delivered systems — absorbing pricing changes without re-architecting, and it never invoices for, or shares in, revenue the customer's application earns from its end users.
statedAs: aiarch invoices the user, usage-based, for hosting of operated systems — no flat subscription, no charge for construction or LLM work; it does not invoice for, or share in, end-user revenue.

aiarch bills the user for hosting of operated systems on a usage-based basis (no flat subscription); construction runs on the user's own Claude Code account and GitHub Actions — aiarch does not charge for construction or LLM work. aiarch is merchant of record only for its own invoices and never touches end-user revenue.

items.statement: All state and source the platform produces for a customer must reside in one customer-owned store per scenario, owned outright and retrievable by the customer at any time.
statedAs: Everything aiarch persists — project state (typed Method models as JSON) and source/charts/manifests — lives in one git target per scenario: the user's own GitHub (via a GitHub App) in the cloud scenarios; aiarch orchestrates via the GitHub API and the user owns the repo and their code outright.

items.statement: The platform orchestrates and observes construction while build, test, and deployment execute on the project's configured construction venue.
statedAs: The platform orchestrates construction; the build/test/push runs on the user's own GitHub Actions (cloud) or a local runner (LOCAL), dispatched and observed by aiarch via the ConstructionPipelineAccess seam.

items.statement: The platform must support pause, replay, override, and human takeover of any in-flight construction activity.
The platform must automatically adjust an Operated System's capacity (scale up, scale down, scale to zero, resume-to-baseline) from observed telemetry, per a customer-tunable policy.
statedAs: The platform must automatically adjust an Operated System's capacity (scale up, scale down, idle-pause, resume-to-baseline) from observed telemetry, per a customer-tunable policy; the autoscaler publishes revised desired state and never drives convergence directly.

items.statement: The platform must expose, for any Operated System, the current cost run-rate, projected monthly cost, and a what-if scale curve, so the Operator and the Customer can see how operating cost responds to load.
Project estimation at SDP-review time must include a usage-to-operating-cost curve and a sensitivity band for ± uncertainty around the customer's declared expected usage, per project option.
statedAs: Project estimation at SDP-review time must include a usage-to-operating-cost curve and a sensitivity band for ± uncertainty around the customer's declared usage assumptions, per project option.

items.statement: The platform must support an evolving, curated set of infrastructure building blocks for deployed customer systems, such that adding or retiring a building block is absorbed without re-architecting.
statedAs: Customer apps deployed by aiarch use a curated, evolving set of infrastructure constituents (launch set: Go + Temporal + Postgres + Git + S3); the supported set evolves and worker generation, autoscaling, and cost projection adapt via Strategy registrations on the affected components.

items.statement: Review gating must be configurable per project: the customer chooses which gates require human approval and which approve automatically, while changes above a risk threshold always require human review.
statedAs: Founder direction (2026-07-20): some customers run 'vibes' (fully automatic); serious customers require human approval at chosen stages; review/approval requirements are configured per customer.

items.name: Project Delivery Workflow
items.rationale: How a project's activities are scheduled and how one activity's task DAG advances: dispatch → collect → review → gate → advance. System design, project design and construction were authored as three separate phase-workflow volatilities, which was a description of the 2026-07 implementation (three Managers, three rails, three UIs) rather than of the business: an agent generates an artifact, agents and humans review it, and the activity advances through its own life cycle (Righting Software App. A) — identically for a Requirements activity, an Architecture activity and a Service activity. Requirements, Architecture and Project Design are activities 1–3 of the project network (Table 11-1), fenced from construction by milestone M0, so there is ONE sequence and ONE axis of change along it: the lifecycle shape per activity type, who must review what, when a human is required, how a send-back re-opens work, and how the pump chooses what runs next. All of that evolves for every customer at once as the Method practice matures, and none of it evolves independently of the rest — the reason three entries were always one.

items.name: Design Conformance Rules
items.rationale: WHICH Method rules judge a draft, and HOW their findings are computed: the rule inventory (counts, layer rules, chain coverage, traceability joins, design↔code alignment, drift) evolves with the Method doctrine release over release, independently of the delivery choreography that asks for the verdict. It was authored as an evaluation facet of the System Design Phase Workflow volatility, which was only ever true of the rail that happened to call it; once the three phase workflows merge, a rule inventory is plainly not a facet of how activities are scheduled. Stands alone so DesignHealthEngine's 1:1 volatility-to-encapsulator relationship is real rather than a shared-facet waiver. Platform-wide, so axis 1.

items.name: Operation Phase Workflow
items.rationale: The choreography by which the platform operates a delivered system — the deploy-after-construction ceremony, reconcile cadence, the health→intervention→autoscale sequencing, delinquency application, withdraw — will evolve as operating practice matures: event-driven reconciliation replacing polled sweeps, progressive-delivery gates (canary, automatic rollback) in the deploy step, self-healing sequences before escalation. Same shape as the Project Delivery Workflow volatility the three Method-phase workflow volatilities merged into: what varies is the Manager's activity sequence, NOT the policies it consults (Intervention Policy, Autoscaling Policy) nor the runtime it drives (Operated Runtime) nor where it records state (Operational State Store). Evolves independently of the delivery phases and of the billing cycle.

items.name: Billing Workflow
items.rationale: The choreography of a billing cycle — read cycle usage, compute the charge, execute the charge, record the outcome, unpaid-charge sweeps, dunning, delinquency escalation — will evolve: dunning sequences, proration on mid-cycle plan changes, pre-authorization holds before large charges. Deliberately distinct from Service Pricing (the pricing policy BillingEngine pivots on — what the charge IS) and from Merchant Gateway Provider (which gateway executes the money movement): what varies here is the cycle's activity sequence itself.

items.name: Construction Estimation Model
items.rationale: How construction duration, cost, and risk are computed will change as agents change, as historical data accumulates, and as the team refines the model. Construction estimation only — the operating-side forecast is split out as Operation Estimation Model. The two evolve on independent timelines (construction estimation matures with agent/build telemetry; operation estimation matures with fleet/usage telemetry).

items.name: Operation Estimation Model
items.rationale: How operating cost is forecasted as a function of usage. Used at design-time (SDP review: usage-to-operating-cost curve + operating-cost sensitivity forecast) and at op-time (OperationsManager: current run-rate, projected monthly cost, what-if curve over observed usage). Evolves as telemetry deepens and as Customer App Infrastructure expands. Independent of Construction Estimation Model because the inputs differ (usage curves + infrastructure cost model vs. build graph + agent throughput) and the outputs serve different decisions.

items.name: Customer App Infrastructure
items.rationale: The list of technologies that a customer's deployed app is permitted to use. Launch set: Go + Temporal + Postgres + Git + S3. The list evolves as the platform broadens (e.g., adding pgvector for AI-feature apps, WASM compute units). The fact of constraint is a design given; the contents of the constrained set is what is volatile — and it broadens for every customer at once. Encapsulated by OperatedRuntimeAccess — the runtime surface through which building blocks reach a customer app — with per-kind Strategy registrations on AutoscalerEngine and OperationEstimationEngine adapting their models as the set evolves.

items.name: Service Pricing
items.rationale: How the platform prices its own service evolves system-wide over time. Current instance: a usage-based hosting fee for operated systems (DEPLOYED — OPERATED); construction currently runs on the customer's own agentic-coding subscription and CI minutes. Tomorrow: per-seat tiers, free-tier subsidies, hosting-resource-class pricing, volume discounts, charges for design/construction work or consulting. This is open-ended, will ripple, and must not be a hardcoded constant — it is the policy billingEngine pivots on as a Strategy. Lives on axis 1 because the platform re-prices its service for everyone as its cost structure and market position change.

items.name: Intervention Policy
items.rationale: What counts as 'stuck', who is notified, when a human is paged, and what authority they have to override is policy that will change as the platform matures. Trigger surface includes construction variance, unhealthy operated state, and billing failures (a user's stored instrument declines a platform service invoice). Early on, every variance escalates to a single operator. Later, severity tiers, customer SLA classes, and self-healing rules emerge.

items.name: Review Policy
items.rationale: At the same moment, different customers run different review policies: one runs fully automatic ('vibes'), another requires human approval at every gate ('full'), a third takes human checkpoints at chosen stages. The policy spans the whole delivery workflow — design-artifact gates and construction change review — and covers both how much work is automated versus human-approved (absorbing the former Construction Hand-Off Policy) and who must review a produced change, from what perspective, against which reference artifacts. A non-overridable risk floor keeps high-risk changes human-reviewed under any preset. The rule set also matures over time, but the dominant axis is per-customer variance at one moment. Encapsulated by ReviewEngine.

items.name: Autoscaling Policy
items.rationale: At the same moment, different operated apps run different capacity policies: SLA-class tiers, per-app scale-to-zero thresholds, scale-from-zero cold-start tolerance, predictive vs. reactive scaling, operator overrides. What counts as 'this app's capacity is right' for one customer's app is wrong for another's. The rule set also matures over time, but the dominant axis is per-app/per-customer policy variance at one moment. Symmetrical with Intervention Policy in shape but structurally distinct: Intervention Policy answers 'is this app broken and what do we do?'; Autoscaling Policy answers 'is this app's capacity right and what do we do?' Two axes, two encapsulators.

items.name: Customer Interaction Channel
items.rationale: Different customers reach the platform through different entry channels at the same moment. Today: a browser hitting the JSON HTTP API, an MCP client (remote MCP over HTTP), and the scheduler's machine-initiated triggers. Tomorrow: IDE plugins, Slack apps, agentic clients, voice. The kind of caller is what varies. Encapsulated by the Client tier — each Client component (WebClient, MCPClient, SchedulerClient) owns one channel's specifics, including its own wire-level transport stack (JSON-over-HTTP today, streaming transports tomorrow), so a channel keeps its identity while its transport changes and Managers never see either.

items.name: Workflow Execution Substrate
items.rationale: Which durable-execution substrate sequences Manager workflow code. Temporal today; other durable executors later — the platform may migrate substrate over its lifetime, and the same Manager code must run unchanged. The executeWorkflow/signal/query/timer/schedule verbs are stable while the runtime behind them varies. Encapsulated by the message-bus utility (deliverSignal + registerSchedule) for cross-Manager control-plane verbs — reworded 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment): durableExecutionAccess was reclassified from a ResourceAccess to this Manager-only Utility at the Task 7b reconciliation (founder ruling R-F); a Manager's own in-workflow primitives are execution substrate per the operational-concepts decision. The embedded test executor is an implementation profile, not a customer-facing axis.

items.name: Agentic Job Venue
items.rationale: Which CI/agentic-pipeline system executes dispatched agentic jobs — Phase-1/2 drafting and Phase-3 construction alike. Current instances: the customer's own GitHub Actions running their agentic-coding tooling, or their local machine's runner; instance set grows (other CI systems, other coding agents); the dry-run/test profile is a stubbed instance behind the same verbs. At one moment different customers run different job targets — it is THEIR venue — and a customer can migrate venue without any Manager change. The submit/observe/cancel verbs are stable; the execution system behind them is what varies. Encapsulated by agenticJobAccess. Split out of the former Durable Execution Runtime axis: the job target varies per customer with their venue choice, while the durable Manager-sequencing substrate varies by platform migration — two independent axes, two encapsulators.

items.name: Operated Runtime
items.rationale: Same shape as Durable Execution Runtime but for the runtime that hosts delivered systems in the DEPLOYED — OPERATED scenario. Today: GitOps over Kubernetes via Argo CD + Argo Rollouts on the platform's hosting cluster. Three faces: convergence infrastructure (how desired-state-in-the-repo becomes actual-state-in-the-cluster), compute cost attribution (per-customer cost-of-goods surface), and runtime-status transport (how the platform learns about state changes in the operated runtime). All three encapsulated behind OperatedRuntimeAccess.

items.name: Source Control Target
items.rationale: At the same moment, different scenarios put the per-project repo — and everything the platform does through it — on different source-control providers/targets. Current instances: the user's own GitHub (via a GitHub App, cloud), the customer's local machine (GitLocal), and an ephemeral throwaway git repo (test); GitLab later. The axis covers both faces of the provider, which co-vary when the provider swaps: (1) the persistence target for typed project state and Phase-3 construction outputs (stable verbs: createProject / readProject / commit / stageArtifact / storeConstructionOutput / retrieveOutputTree), and (2) the provider's collaboration/authorization surface (app installation and tokens, secrets, branch protection, branches, pull requests, reviews, merges). One axis fronted by three ResourceAccess components under the ratified facet doctrine (see operational concepts), one per stable verb family: projectStateAccess (typed state), artifactAccess (construction outputs), sourceControlAccess (collaboration/authorization). The former 'GitHubAppLifecycle' is a mechanism of the current GitHub instance, not an axis of change.

items.name: Merchant Gateway Provider
items.rationale: Which merchant gateway executes the platform's money movement — charging customers for cycle amounts and validating stored instruments. Stripe today (charge-only); the platform may change or add providers over its lifetime. The verbs are stable (chargeCustomer / validateStoredInstrument); the gateway behind them — its idempotency mechanics and webhook shapes — is what varies. Encapsulated by merchantGatewayAccess.

items.name: Operational State Store
items.rationale: Which storage substrate holds the platform's own operational records — operated-system state, billing state, usage log, and (2026-08-02) the episode ledger. Postgres for state/usage/billing, a local gitignored sidecar for episode traces today; managed alternatives and a deployed episode profile later, potentially migrating per record family over the platform's lifetime. The atomic business verbs on each record family are stable; the substrate behind them — engine, consistency mechanics, hosting — is what varies. One axis fronted by four ResourceAccess components, one per verb family: operatedSystemStateAccess, billingStateAccess, usageAccess, episodeAccess (ratified facet doctrine — see operational concepts). Deliberately distinct from Source Control Target: transactional row/append stores, not the per-project git repo.

rejected.name: Customer Interaction Transport
rejected.reason: Folded into Customer Interaction Channel (2026-07-22): wire mechanics for a fixed caller kind never ripple past the single Client component that owns the channel — each Client owns its own transport stack, so a separate system-level entry added noise. SchedulerClient re-tagged as a Channel binding.

rejected.name: Construction Hand-Off Policy
rejected.reason: Folded into Review Policy (2026-07-22): how much work is automated versus human-approved is the same per-customer policy the review presets (vibes/checkpoints/full) configure; a separate volatility and its HandOffEngine encapsulator duplicated ReviewEngine's axis. HandOffEngine retired with it.

rejected.name: Work Tracking
rejected.reason: Descoped by founder ruling (2026-07-20): the customer's external work-item tracker is not a platform concern; programmatic extensibility (objective 8 — agents over MCP, apps over the API) is the surface through which external trackers can sync. WorkItemAccess and WorkItemTracker removed with it.

rejected.name: System Design Phase Workflow
rejected.reason: Merged into Project Delivery Workflow (2026-09-23, spec §4): system design, project design and construction are one activity sequence fenced by M0 (R1), so their choreography varies on one axis, not three. Its rule-evaluation facet — which Method rules judge a draft — split out as the stand-alone Design Conformance Rules volatility instead of riding along.

rejected.name: Project Design Phase Workflow
rejected.reason: Merged into Project Delivery Workflow (2026-09-23, spec §4): under R7 project design is deterministic — one review task (SDP Review · M0) over an engine-computed artifact — so there is no separate drafting choreography left to vary. The estimation model it used to carry remains its own volatility (Construction Estimation Model).

rejected.name: Construction Phase Workflow
rejected.reason: Merged into Project Delivery Workflow (2026-09-23, spec §4): per-activity execution choreography is the SAME choreography the design activities run, differing only in data (the lifecycle) and strategy (command, worker class, artifact codec) — never in a branch on design-vs-construction (spec §5.2).

waivers.justification: WAIVED (Refreshed 2026-09-23 (stage-1 model wave)): 18 volatilities — 12 same-customer-over-time, 6 all-customers-at-one-moment — still over the 6-15 target. Down from 19: the three phase-workflow volatilities (System Design / Project Design / Construction) merged into one Project Delivery Workflow, and DesignHealthEngine's rule inventory split out as the stand-alone Design Conformance Rules; both moves are recorded in the volatilities rejected ledger. Every remaining entry has exactly one named encapsulator and requirement traces: the last ratified facet group — SystemDesignManager, ProjectDesignManager and ConstructionManager sharing Project Delivery Workflow, waived here as explicitly transitional — ENDED at stage 4a, where delivery-manager became that volatility's 1:1 encapsulator. Only Managers may call it (arch-test import rule). A parent pump workflow per project starts a child activity-lifecycle workflow for every eligible activity (R3); the child is one generic DAG walker whose per-type differences are DATA (the method-assets lifecycle) and STRATEGY (command, worker class, artifact codec), never a branch on design-versus-construction. waivers.guideline: Golden Engines-to-Managers ratio — fewer Engines than Managers (the book's expectation).
waivers.justification: WAIVED (Refreshed 2026-07-22 (reconciliation)): 7 Engines against 5 Managers still inverts the book's ~3-for-5 ratio. HandOffEngine was retired (hand-off policy folded into Review Policy / ReviewEngine). Remaining consolidation candidates examined and rejected: EstimationEngine + OperationEstimationEngine encapsulate two independently-evolving estimation models with disjoint caller sets; InterventionEngine + AutoscalerEngine encapsulate distinct policies with different reuse profiles. Each of the 7 Engines has a 1:1 volatility-to-encapsulator relationship. design-health-engine joined the Engine set 2026-08-01 (founder ruling R-F: its call carries the ci-check business verdict in uc1's chain — an evaluation Strategy, not ambient infrastructure); since 2026-09-23 it is the SOLE owner of the Design Conformance Rules volatility, so its 1:1 relationship no longer rests on a shared System Design Phase Workflow facet. Re-evaluate at the next scope-change replan.

waivers.guideline: Engine names are gerunds (ch. 3 naming rule: gerund + Engine suffix, e.g. MatchingEngine).
waivers.justification: WAIVED (Refreshed 2026-07-22 (reconciliation)): 6 of 7 Engines are noun-named rather than gerund-named (EstimationEngine, OperationEstimationEngine, InterventionEngine, AutoscalerEngine, ReviewEngine, DesignHealthEngine; only BillingEngine conforms). The rule is a readability convention, not a structural one. Renaming cascades through component ids, serviceContracts keys, and Go packages while construction is active — apply gerund names opportunistically whenever an architectural change next touches a given Engine's contract.

attestations.guideline: Never design against requirements; design against volatility.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: decomposition follows the 19-item volatilities slot; no component is named after a feature, use case, or domain noun; every component blurb cites its volatility. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Avoid functional decomposition — no container or component named after a feature.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: component roster contains no feature-named containers (no *Processing, *Reporting, per-use-case services). Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Decompose based on volatility — every component cites a volatilities entry.
attestations.justification: Refreshed 2026-07-22 (reconciliation): every Manager, Engine, and ResourceAccess carries an encapsulates citation into the 19-item volatilities slot; Customer Interaction Channel is bound by the three Client components and Customer App Infrastructure is owned by OperatedRuntimeAccess (recorded in both the volatility rationale and the component blurb). Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Composable design — non-core use cases trace through existing components without modification.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: all 11 non-core variations trace through existing components without modification — each carries its own step-keyed dynamic-view realization in the committed System (the founder's total-coverage extension), none required a new component. Smallest-set (ch. 4) extension, attested 2026-07-30: at 37 components the roster still exceeds the book's dozen-or-two guidance, but the smallest-set discipline was applied directly in the 2026-07-22 reconciliation that consolidated 43→37 (HandOffEngine cut; the four facet ResourceAccess folded into ProjectStateAccess; RevenueLedgerAccess folded into BillingStateAccess) — each cut a diminishing-returns judgment that a separate component encapsulated no distinct volatility. The residual size is consciously carried by the §2d ratio waiver, and further shrink awaits subsystem partitioning. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment): wording updated to step-keyed realization language — all 16 dynamic views (core + variation) now carry realized step tables, none required a new component.

attestations.guideline: Features as integration, not implementation — no Manager named for a feature.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: the 5 Managers are named for phase workflow families, not features; features arrive as integration (new step-keyed realizations), not new components. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment): wording updated to step-keyed realization language — the coverage reconciliation's two retroactive activities (C-AA, C-DH) and the align-up rail calls are both integration onto existing components, not new ones.

Attested 2026-07-22 (Phase-1 half): design IS iterative here — the draft→critique→review→amend loop with staleness propagation is the mechanism; the build-incrementally half is Phase-3's. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Volatility decreases top-down through the layers.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: volatility decreases top-down — Managers encapsulate workflow choreography (most volatile), Engines policies/models, ResourceAccess substrate mechanics, Resources/Utilities the most stable. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment): the earlier "durableExecution 4" RA multi-service example is stale — durableExecutionAccess was reclassified to the message-bus Utility at the Task 7b reconciliation (founder ruling R-F) and no longer sits in the ResourceAccess layer; replaced with the two live RA examples the align-up batch itself just confirmed exercised by 3 Managers apiece (projectStateAccess: system-design-manager, project-design-manager, construction-manager; sourceControlAccess: the same three, post align-up).

Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

model.notes: Team: solo founder (bus-factor-1) + up to 3 concurrent Claude agent streams (architect/PM/product-manager/specialist roles). Founder works ~2 effective days/week (40% of nominal). Parallelism cap: 3 in-flight agent streams; beyond that, founder review quality degrades. Infrastructure: Go + Temporal + Postgres (CNPG for Temporal + billing head-state only; project state is JSON-in-git with git-ref CAS). Construction CI is the user's own GitHub Actions running claude-code-action — the platform holds no LLM key and does not charge for construction. Billing model (2026-06-09 MoR-reversal): pure one-directional vendor charge — the platform bills the user a usage-based HOSTING fee only (DEPLOYED — OPERATED scenario); no flat subscription; no charge for construction or LLM work. The platform bills a usage-based hosting fee for operating a delivered system and nothing else. Revenue share was reversed on 2026-06-09 and is no longer part of the vocabulary (stage 4b2, founder ruling): the concept is gone rather than set to zero, because a field whose UNKNOWN member had to stand in for 'none' could not state the platform's actual posture. computeCost=2 (tieredFloors: tier floors + free-tier subsidies per ServicePricing strategy); schedule=1 (monthly billing period). Risk flags: bus-factor-1; founder availability variable (2d/wk); operated runtime unchosen; durable execution platform unchosen; git-as-project-state-store novelty; AI-agent construction quality variance; dog-food chicken-and-egg. No hard external deadlines. Internal-only v1 audience.

activityExecutionAccess.title: activityExecutionAccess contract
activityExecutionAccess.notes: The one staging -> review -> commit verb family for EVERY activity, and the owner of the two append-only per-activity ledgers (Attempts, Reviews). Added ADDITIVELY in stage 3 task 3 over three facets it supersedes. constructionTransitionAccess is DELETED (dct Plan 4 Task 3, spec §11 ruling A5 — there is no production usage, so no in-flight history to protect): its activity-scoped callers moved onto these verbs (RecordActivityExited + RecordActivityFailed → RecordActivityOutcome, RecordOperatorNote + RecordOperatorNoteDelivered → RecordOperatorNote, RecordChangeReviewed dropped because the review is the round DecideReviewRound records), and its three project-scoped writes moved to projectStateAccess. gitActivityStatusAccess and designSessionAccess keep only the ops with live callers (their own notes list them). RecordActivityOutcome is the one verb besides OpenActivity that may BIRTH a row: a FAILURE recorded with no activity-version expectation against an activity that has no row (the pump's blocked verdict — an unclassifiable activity or an unresolvable dependency has nothing to open) creates the row it fails, exactly as the retired RecordActivityFailed did; an outcome without a failure reason, or any expectation, still requires the row. RecordOperatorNote STAMPS DELIVERY ON A RE-RECORD: re-recording a note that is already held with identical content and a deliveredToAttemptID stamps it delivered to that attempt if it was not yet delivered, is a no-op if it was delivered to the same attempt, and is refused (ContractMisuse) if it was delivered to another — the fold of the retired note/delivery pair, so the dispatch that carries a gate's note marks it delivered without a second verb. NO SEPARATE COMMIT LANE. Spec 5.3 asks for a project-scoped serialized lane {projectId}:statewrite; it is deliberately NOT built, because applyMutationOnBranchFiles already is one: it fetches the branch tip fresh per call, probes the idempotency ledger BEFORE the version guard, and commits project.json plus the dedup record in ONE git commit CAS'd against the observed base, so git's ref update is the cross-process gate on both substrates. A CAS loss surfaces as fwra.Conflict, which is Temporal-retryable, and the workflow already carries the re-read -> re-apply loop. A second durable singleton per project is exactly the shape the pump-singular-per-project fix had to clean up. Per-activity Version (task 4) is an additional in-document guard inside the transition, not a lane; {projectId}:statewrite is earmarked for stage 4, where the parallel pump actually raises contention. REOPEN IS A REQUEUE NOTE, NOT A THIRTEENTH VERB (stage 4b1 task 12). Terminal was terminal and nothing could undo it: OpenActivity refuses an exited row ('a finished activity is not re-opened in place'), StartedAt/CompletedAt/FailureReason/FailureDetail are write-once, and the pump's eligibility refuses any row a pump has written - so a failed walk, a spent variance budget or an operator's Skip left an activity NOTHING could ever re-run, and the operator's only recovery was an amendment minting a new activity id. RecordOperatorNote of kind REQUEUE now re-arms such a row: it clears exactly those four head facts and preserves everything that makes the activity's history readable (both ledgers, the lifecycle pin, the classified type/variant, produced artifacts, operator notes), so the next walk re-seeds the tasks that passed and re-dispatches only what did not. A requeue against a row that has NOT exited is refused - there is nothing to requeue, and re-arming a live row would hand a second child the row this one is writing. WHY A FOLD AND NOT A NEW OP, measured rather than assumed: a thirteenth verb here puts this facet past App-C's op ceiling of 12 and fires DH-CONTRACT-OPCOUNT-MAX, which the committed state's own advisory pin asserts ABSENT (designhealth TestGreenFixtureAdvisoriesFire: 'the largest surviving contract is 12 ... the FIRST time the repo has had no Manager contract past App-C's ceiling'). The requeue kind was already in the OperatorNoteKind vocabulary with no writer, an operator's re-open is exactly the decision that verb records, and folding makes the audit entry and the re-arm ONE commit - so a crash can no longer leave a re-armed activity with nobody's name on it, which two ops could.

jsonPath.description: Where the comment is anchored in the artifact under review, as a JSONPath.

noteId.description: The caller's deterministic id for this note. Recording the same id again with identical content changes nothing, except that a re-record carrying a deliveredToAttemptID stamps a not-yet-delivered note delivered to that attempt (and is refused if the note was delivered to another); with different content it is refused.

gate.description: The gate the note was written at: a lifecycle phase's wire name, "merge" or "takeover"; empty when none applies.

text.description: The operator's note, verbatim. Must not be blank.

comments.description: Anchored comments that ride with the note.

OperatorNoteKind.description: Why an operator wrote a note, i.e. the gate or steer it rode on: 1 sendBack (a phase gate's SendBack feedback), 2 retry, 3 takeover, 4 reassign, 5 skip (recorded, never delivered: nothing runs after a skip), 6 requeue. 0 is the unknown sentinel and is refused. REQUEUE IS THE ONE KIND THAT CHANGES THE ROW. On activityExecutionAccess (the one facet that records notes since constructionTransitionAccess was deleted) a requeue against an activity that has EXITED RE-ARMS the row: the four sticky head facts (startedAt, completedAt, failureReason, failureDetail) are cleared in the same commit as the note, both ledgers and the lifecycle pin are kept, and the pump selects the activity again because the note itself is the evidence it reads. It is refused against a row that has not exited. Every other kind is a steer of work in flight and leaves the row's own facts alone.

TestingVariant.description: The sub-type of a testing (N-*) activity. 0 is None: the value every non-testing activity carries, so it can cross a Temporal payload; it is NOT a testing variant. Ordinal 0 was Plan (N-STP) and 3 was SystemTest (N-IT) until 2026-10-02 (deterministic component testing, spec §7): neither is a testing variant again, and 3 is never reused.

typeKey.description: The lifecycles.json type key whose task DAG this activity runs. Pinned at open so a method-assets release landing mid-flight cannot re-shape an activity that is already running.

assetsVersion.description: The method-assets release the type key was resolved against, recorded verbatim so a later reader can tell which lifecycle shape the ledger below was written under.

LifecyclePin.description: What an activity's task DAG was pinned to when it opened.

activityId.description: The activity whose task output was staged.

taskId.description: The lifecycle task whose output was staged.

branch.description: The branch the output was staged on; empty means the project's default branch.

version.description: The project-state version the staging commit produced — the same token every other verb on this contract returns, carried INSIDE the ref because the contract dialect admits exactly one result per operation.

StagedRef.description: Where one task's staged output landed, and at which state version.

attemptId.description: The deterministic "<activityId>:<taskId>:<n>" id (projectstate.AttemptID). Recording it twice appends once — the episode ledger's TargetRef joins on this exact string, so its format is frozen.

taskId.description: The Figure A-1 task this attempt executed.

outcome.description: The attempt's terminal state; pending while it is still running.

evidenceKind.description: What the evidence ref points at.

evidenceRef.description: The evidence itself — a commit, an episode id, an artifact ref.

detail.description: The attempt's own render-ready sentence, verbatim, or empty where the attempt has nothing to say beyond its outcome. NOT required: an empty detail is the honest answer for an attempt that did exactly what its task says. Recorded on the append and carried unchanged on the resolve.

TaskAttemptInput.description: One execution of one lifecycle task, as the caller states it. The store denormalises the phase, stamps the clock and the provenance, and appends.

SubjectKind.description: What a review round is judging.

ref.description: The subject itself: a commit sha, an artifact kind's wire name, or a pull-request ref.

SubjectRef.description: The exact thing a review round judged — without it a verdict cites nothing.

role.description: The reviewer's Method role (architect, productManager, qaEngineer, ...).

actor.description: The agent or person filling that role for this round.

required.description: Whether the round cannot be decided passed without this reviewer's verdict.

RoundReviewer.description: One seat on a round's reviewer roster, as the reviewEngine computed it.

VerdictKind.description: One reviewer's judgement. It is NOT the round's outcome — the round is decided separately, by DecideReviewRound.

reviewerRole.description: The roster role this verdict was cast under.

attemptId.description: The attempt this verdict judged, by its AttemptID — the join back to the ledger and to that attempt's episode.

at.description: RFC3339, stamped by the store, never by the caller. Empty on input.

ReviewVerdict.description: One reviewer's judgement inside a round, appended with its comments in ONE commit.

ReviewRoundOutcome.description: A round's terminal state. Pending is the zero value: a round that has verdicts but has not been decided.

roundId.description: The deterministic, caller-minted round id. The construction rail mints "<activityId>:<reviewTaskId>:<n>"; the DESIGN rails mint "<activityId>:<reviewTaskId>:<artifactKind>:<n>", because several artifact kinds share one lifecycle phase (mission and glossary; system and operationalConcepts) and a three-part id would collide across two independent design sessions. The shape is the caller's; the rule this store enforces is that opening the same id twice opens ONE round — the property the whole ledger rests on under Temporal retry.

taskId.description: The REVIEW task this round is an attempt of.

reviews.description: The work task this round judges.

artifactKind.description: The artifact this round judges, when the round is about one. PRESENT on a design round and ABSENT on a construction round, whose subject is a commit rather than a slot model. The caller supplies it; the store stores it verbatim, and write-once: re-opening a round id under a different kind is the caller contradicting itself about what this round judges.

reviewers.description: The roster, as the reviewEngine computed it at open time.

ReviewRoundInput.description: A review round as the caller opens it. Everything after open is appended.

taskId.description: The REVIEW task this round is an attempt of.

reviews.description: The work task this round judges.

artifactKind.description: The artifact this round judges, when the round is about one. PRESENT on a design round and ABSENT on a construction round, whose subject is a commit rather than a slot model. It is a FIELD for two reasons. A review task's ID does not determine what it judges: `designReview` names a task in eight lifecycles and `testing` in nine, each carrying no artifactKind of its own and resolving its subject through `reviews`, so a round keyed (taskId, round) alone can only be resolved by re-fetching the activity's lifecycle. And several artifact kinds are designed to share one lifecycle phase — the four-part design RoundID exists for exactly that — so the day one gate task judges two kinds, a reader that joins on (taskId, round) binds both into one revision. The kind is ALSO inside that RoundID, and nothing may parse a RoundID: this is the field that makes the join honest. ABSENT on a round written before this field existed, which the readers treat as the legacy case it is rather than as a construction round.

verdicts.description: Append-only: every verdict cast in this round, in the order cast.

thread.description: The round's anchored comment thread, normalised by the same ApplyReviewBatch the artifact ledger uses.

outcome.description: Pending until DecideReviewRound stamps it; terminal after.

decidedBy.description: Who decided the round; empty while pending.

openedAt.description: RFC3339, stamped by the store at open.

decidedAt.description: RFC3339, stamped by the store at decide; empty while pending.

provenance.description: Where this round's record came from, in the same closed vocabulary an attempt carries: observed for a live write, backfilled for one the migration reconstructed (which must name its basis), synthesized for one derived from nothing. Without it a reconstructed round reads exactly like a recorded one, which is the single worst lie this ledger could tell.

ReviewRound.description: One append-only review round: its subject, its roster, its verdicts, its thread, and — once — its decision.

result.description: The whole stored execution record for one activity: the lifecycle pin and the head facts (type, variant, started, completed, failure) beside the two append-only ledgers, its produced artifacts, its operator notes and its per-activity version. Bound through x-go-type rather than a $def because the stored row carries omitempty head facts the schema dialect cannot express — a not-required $ref emits a pointer, a required one emits a member on every row — and the stored shape is the one thing this wave must keep byte-exact. The same seam the attempt ledger already uses (x-go-type []TaskAttempt).

RoutingDirective.description: Cycle routing under charge-only terms: NoAction (0) or Charge (2). Wire value 1 (the retired payout arm) is tombstoned — never reuse.

closed.description: The period has been closed and its outcome recorded.

escalated.description: The charge failed and was escalated: the customer is persistently delinquent and the cycle's invoice unpaid.

RoutingDirective.description: Cycle routing under charge-only terms: NoAction (0) or Charge (2). Wire value 1 (the retired payout arm) is tombstoned — never reuse.

Settled.description: True once the cycle's close recorded its outcome (settleCycle); false while the period is open.

BillingCycle.description: One billing cycle as head state records it: the settled outcome of its close, or Settled=false (zero outcome) while it is open.

ProjectID.description: The project the customer is billed for: the link a DelinquencyScope narrows ReadPersistentlyDelinquentCustomers by. Empty = registered under no project (only a platform-wide sweep, an empty scope, finds the customer).

CustomerProfile.description: Charge-only customer profile — the registration attributes. Carries no payout/connected-account fields.

ProjectID.description: Narrows the sweep to the customers registered under this project (CustomerProfile.ProjectID). Empty = every persistently delinquent customer (platform-wide).

GatewayCustomerRef.description: The merchant gateway’s customer / stored-instrument reference (charge-only; replaces the retired ConnectedAccountID)

RoutingDirective.description: Cycle routing under charge-only terms: NoAction (0) or Charge (2). Wire value 1 (the retired payout arm) is tombstoned — never reuse.

ActivityConstructionPhase.description: The coarse per-activity construction lifecycle, DERIVED from the row's head facts and its resolved phase completions — never stored. Member 4 (completedNotLanded) is APPENDED: ordinals 0-3 are wire values in every committed project and this model renumbers nothing.

Variant.description: The testing variant of a testing activity; absent on every other row (the zero value is no variant, and ordinals 0 and 3 are retired).

Phase.description: The coarse lifecycle-phase roll-up. Meaningless when hasBuildEvidence is false (or classified is false): nothing has been resolved to roll up, so the value is the enum's zero, not a reported phase. Read it only when both flags are true.

BuildStatus.description: The coarse build status. Meaningless when hasBuildEvidence is false (or classified is false): its zero value names InConstruction, which on such a row reports nothing, not work in progress. Read it only when both flags are true.

recorded.description: True iff a stored .activityExecution head-state row exists for this activity. False on a planned-no-record row: one the server emits because the committed activity list names the activity but nothing has been recorded for it yet. Such a row carries no attempts and no worstOrigin, and its BuildStatus and Phase are meaningless.

worstOrigin.description: The least-trustworthy provenance origin across attempts (synthesized, then backfilled, then observed). Omitted when recorded is false. Meaningless when attempts is empty: the roll-up seeds an empty ledger to observed, which says nothing was derived from anything unknown, not that anything was observed.

pendingResume.description: Present iff no construction pump opened this row (no start stamp) yet its attempt ledger resolves some lifecycle phases complete and others not: an integration-pending row the backfill recorded. It is NOT in flight (nothing is running it) and it is not under review. Omitted on every other row: not started, pump-written, and done.

operatorNotes.description: Every note an operator recorded against this activity (a send-back's feedback, a steer's reason), append-only and in recorded order. A note is pending until an agent dispatch carries it whole; then it names that dispatch's attempt. Delivery is at-least-once: when a note's delivery stamp cannot be written, the note stays pending and the next attempt carries it again, so an agent may see one note twice but never zero times, and never twice in the same attempt. When the pending notes exceed the 16 KiB one dispatch carries, the oldest wait for a later attempt so the newest arrives whole. A note recorded where no agent runs next (a merge-only retry, a takeover, or a finished activity) stays pending until the activity's next agent dispatch. Omitted when there are none.

id.description: The lifecycle phase's wire name: requirements, detailed_design, test_plan, construction or integration.

weight.description: The share of the activity's progress this lifecycle phase carries; the weights of one activity sum to 100.

gateTaskId.description: The review task whose pass IS this lifecycle phase's binary exit criterion.

completed.description: True iff the gate task's state is passed.

id.description: The task id within the lifecycle (a Figure A-1 task id for a construction activity).

phase.description: The id of the lifecycle phase this task belongs to.

dependsOn.description: The task ids that must pass before this one may start. Two tasks that share a predecessor run in parallel; a task with several waits for all of them.

reviews.description: For a review task, the dispatch task it judges — the pair a send-back re-opens. Omitted on a dispatch task.

revisions.description: Oldest first. A dispatch task and the review task that judges it share revision numbers.

reviewSet.description: Who reviews the artifact at THIS task's gate. Present only while this task is awaiting a human decision. On a fork two tasks are awaiting at once and the review engine answers each separately, so the roster is a per-task fact: it was on the activity until stage 4b3, where it could only ever describe whichever gate was entered last.

reviewSetError.description: Why reviewSet is absent at this task's live gate: the review engine refused the proposal. It is a defect in the Manager's call or in the engine, never an operator error, and the gate itself is unaffected — Approve and SendBack work. Omitted when the engine answered or this task has no live gate.

awaitingSince.description: When THIS occurrence of the task's human stage began, in workflow time. A send-back's redraft re-enters the gate with a new awaitingSince, so the pair (task id, awaitingSince) identifies one gate occurrence. Omitted whenever the task is not awaiting a human.

awaitingUntil.description: When an escalation on this task stops waiting and fails the activity: awaitingSince plus the escalation-wait window. Omitted for phase approval gates and for an escalation that waits indefinitely.

redraftExhausted.description: True when THIS task's gate can take no further SendBack redraft: a gate redrafts at most 4 times and refuses the fifth send-back, so approve it, or steer the activity with OverrideActivity. Recomputed on entry to every gate occurrence; false whenever the task has no live gate.

ActivityView.description: One activity's lifecycle, per-task revisions and live review set: the Activity Experience's single read. Derived on read from the attempt ledger, the episode ledger, the operator notes, the stored lifecycle-phase completions and the live session; nothing here is stored.

name.description: The activity's display title from the committed activity list; its id when the list carries no title.

type.description: The activity type's wire name: service, frontend, testing, deployment, documentation, uiDesign or integration.

variant.description: The testing variant's wire name (plan, harness, perf, systemTest or qaProcess). Omitted unless type is testing.

componentId.description: The architecture component this activity builds. Omitted for an activity with none (the system test plan, system testing).

phases.description: The lifecycle phases (Figure A-2) in lifecycle order.

tasks.description: Every task of the lifecycle DAG, in lifecycle order — including the tasks nothing has happened on yet. The reviewer roster and the awaiting facts live HERE, on the task, since stage 4b3: a fork has two gates open at once and an activity-level answer could only ever name one of them.

AwaitingTaskGate.description: ONE task's live human gate, as the activity's own execution sees it. It is the plural replacement for ConstructionSessionView's six flat gate members: those described an ACTIVITY while the facts are per TASK, so on a fork — where a service activity holds detailed_design and test_plan at once — they could only ever name whichever gate was entered last, and two stage 4b2 call sites read them and got the fork wrong. The key IS the task: there is one entry per task awaiting a human right now, and none at all when nobody is being waited on.

taskId.description: The lifecycle task id this entry is about, or "merge" for the local merge hold. It is the key a decision must address.

gate.description: The gate CLASS this occurrence waits at: the task's own id for a phase approval, "merge" for the merge hold, "takeover" for an escalation. It is NOT redundant with taskId — an escalation is keyed by the task that escalated and waits at "takeover".

reviewSet.description: Who reviews the artifact at this task's gate. Absent when no roster went up: an escalation and the merge hold ask no reviewer set, and a refusal explains itself in reviewSetError.

reviewSetError.description: Why reviewSet is absent at this gate: the review engine refused the proposal. It is a defect in the Manager's call or in the engine, never an operator error, and the gate itself is unaffected — Approve and SendBack work. Omitted whenever the engine answered.

awaitingSince.description: When THIS occurrence of the task's human stage began, in workflow time. A send-back's redraft re-enters the gate with a new awaitingSince, so the pair (taskId, awaitingSince) identifies one occurrence.

awaitingUntil.description: When an escalation stops waiting and fails the activity: awaitingSince plus the escalation-wait window. Omitted for a phase approval gate and for the merge hold.

redraftExhausted.description: True when this gate can take no further SendBack redraft: its human-paced budget is spent, so approve it or steer the activity with OverrideActivity. Recomputed on entry to every gate occurrence; false at the merge hold and at an escalation.

awaitingTasks.description: Every task this activity is awaiting a human at right now, sorted by task id so a replayed query reproduces it. Empty when nobody is being waited on. It REPLACES the six flat gate members (reviewSet, reviewSetError, awaitingGate, awaitingSince, awaitingUntil, redraftExhausted), which named one gate for a whole activity and were therefore wrong on any fork.

attempt.description: The current supervision attempt, 1-based: a variance retry, an operator Retry and an escalation's re-dispatch each start the next one. 0 before the first attempt and on the project-level view.

attemptBudget.description: How many supervision attempts the activity gets before it fails with VarianceExhausted, so a client never hardcodes the number. 0 on the project-level view.

DeliveryTestRunView.description: The testing task's run as the results panel renders it: the recorded run, every projected scenario joined with its result, the projected ids with no result (missing), the results with no projected scenario (unknown), and whether the venue artifact has expired.

jsonPath.description: Where the comment is anchored in the artifact under review, as a JSONPath.

gate.description: The gate the note was written at: a lifecycle phase's wire name, "merge" or "takeover". Omitted when none applies.

comments.description: Anchored comments that rode with the note. Omitted when there are none.

recordedAt.description: When the store recorded the note (server clock).

deliveredToAttemptId.description: The AttemptID ("<activityId>:<task>:<n>", the TargetRef of that dispatch's episode) of the agent dispatch that carried this note. Omitted while the note is pending (never set for a note the dispatch carried only in part), and always for a skip note, which nothing runs after.

deliveredAt.description: When the delivery was recorded. Omitted while the note is pending.

OperatorNoteKind.description: Why an operator wrote a note: 1 sendBack (a phase gate's SendBack feedback), 2 retry, 3 takeover, 4 reassign, 5 skip (recorded, never delivered), 6 requeue.

PendingDependency.description: One unsatisfied direct dependency of an integration-pending row.

id.description: The dependency id as the network authors it: an activity id or a milestone id.

reason.description: Why it is unsatisfied. notBuilt: an activity that is not Done. builtNotIntegrated: an activity that is itself integration-pending. milestoneNotReached: a milestone whose own dependencies are not all satisfied. unresolved: an id naming neither an activity nor a milestone, or a milestone cycle (a plan defect).

PendingResume.description: Where an integration-pending row resumes, and what it waits on first.

fromPhase.description: The first lifecycle phase of the row's profile that its resolved phase set does not hold complete: the phase the pump would run first.

waitsOn.description: The row's direct network dependencies that are not satisfied, in authored order. Empty when every dependency is satisfied: the row is next in line.

activityExecution.description: One view row per activity, keyed by ActivityID — the stored .activityExecution rows plus a planned-no-record row for every activity the committed list names and nothing has been recorded for. Renamed from ActivityConstruction in stage-3 task 4 with the stored map it projects: the row's derived members (Phase, Phases, CurrentPhase, Kind, BuildStatus) are COMPUTED here from the two ledgers and are no longer stored anywhere. The view type keeps its own name until the stage-5 Activity Experience replaces it wholesale.

constructionStarted.description: True iff construction has started for this project: some stored .activityExecution row carries a head fact only the construction pump writes (a start stamp, an exit stamp, or a recorded failure) or an attempt of origin observed. Reconstructed attempts (backfilled or synthesized) never count, and a planned-no-record row has no stored state to count. Decides Begin versus Resume.

operatorPaused.description: True while an operator's pause of this project's construction is recorded (PauseProject); cleared by ResumeProject. Every construction pump honours it, the 30-second sweep skips the project, and Begin (ExecuteNextActivity) is refused until it is cleared: the console offers Resume instead.

pauseReason.description: The reason the operator gave when pausing construction. Omitted when construction is not paused.

activityIds.description: Every activity this pump tick dispatched, in the order the frontier pass selected them. Empty when the tick dispatched nothing (a quiescent frontier, a recorded pause, or an activity already in flight).

PumpStatus.description: Whether the project's one construction pump is running now. It is one fact, deliberately separate from the recorded operator pause and from any activity's live session: a client combines them.

open.description: True iff the project's one construction pump ({projectId}:nextActivity) has a RUNNING execution now. A pump cascading between activities reads as open (it continues as new under the same id). False when no pump has run for the project, or the last one closed (it drained quiet, was paused, or failed).

runStartedAt.description: When the pump's CURRENT run started. A cascading pump starts a new run for every activity it dispatches, so this is the current run's start, not the cascade's. Omitted when the pump is not open.

role.description: The reviewer's Method role (architect, productManager, qaEngineer, ...).

actor.description: The agent or person filling that role for this round.

required.description: Whether the round could not be decided passed without this reviewer's verdict.

requiresHuman.description: Whether the review engine requires a human decision at this gate. Display-only on the session view: the enforced gate is the suspend itself.

reason.description: The engine's one-line explanation of the gate verdict (preset, policy row, non-overridable floor, or the project-design spend floor). Omitted when the engine refused to propose.

kind.description: What the ref names — the ledger's own closed vocabulary (projectstate.SubjectKind), carried through unchanged. Both live rails mint commit (the staged model's sha on the design rail, the pushed work's sha on the construction rail) as of 38fd7f9c; pullRequest is what a reviewer's PR is recorded as, and artifact is the ref of an artifact judged outside either rail.

ref.description: What the round judged: the staged commit sha, the pull request a reviewer opens, or the artifact's own ref. The artifact AS OF a revision is a git read of this ref — no second copy is stored.

status.description: Derived by the store from the comment's replies; carried through verbatim so the screen shows what the reviewer left behind.

type.description: What the comment asks of its addressee: a change, an answer, or an acknowledgement that the thing it was anchored to has moved on.

ReviewVerdictKind.description: One reviewer's answer in a round. Agent and human verdicts are the same kind of row; abstain is a reviewer who was asked and declined, which is not silence.

actor.description: The agent or person who gave it. Omitted when the role alone identifies the reviewer.

at.description: RFC3339, stamped by the store when the verdict was appended, verbatim. A string and not a date-time: the ledger holds it as one, and parsing it here would turn an unstamped legacy verdict into the zero instant.

attemptId.description: The gate attempt this verdict was given at.

DesignArtifactSessionStage.description: The stages the DERIVED design-artifact session view can report, and all of them. DesignArtifactSessionView.description: The ONE derived session view, for all seventeen artifact kinds (stage 4b2). It is a projection of the durable slot, NOT a live session: its subject is what the slot says now, and the live execution's view is constructionSession, a different subject with a different lifetime. Eight members were pruned with the type's rename because nothing in the server could set them once 4b1 retired the live design rail — they were decoded by the SPA and always absent.

via.description: The alternative callers when an alt group's calls into the component collapse to this one stimulus (Amendment A4); empty when the stimulus has a single caller.

ScenarioView.description: One deterministic scenario projected onto a component (framework-go/scenario.ForComponent): the stimuli into it, what is observed after each, and the committed binding for it when the test plan has one.

detail.description: The attempt's own render-ready sentence, verbatim. Absent where the attempt recorded none.

TaskRevisionOutcome.description: A revision's rendered outcome. `withdrawn` is a round pulled back before anyone decided it — deliberate, not a fault, which is why it is not `failed`; `skipped` is a gate the policy did not hold for a human.

TaskRevisionProvenance.description: The worst origin among the revision's attempts: synthesized if any was fabricated, else backfilled if any was reconstructed from evidence recorded elsewhere, else observed.

n.description: 1-based. Revision n is the n-th work that reached the gate, with every failed or retried attempt before it, and the n-th gate attempt that judged it.

endedAt.description: Omitted while any attempt of the revision is unresolved.

attemptIds.description: Every attempt of the revision, as "<activityId>:<task>:<n>" — the TargetRef of each attempt's episode. More than one means the work was retried before it reached the gate.

episodeId.description: The episode of the attempt that reached the gate (else the latest). Omitted on a review task and where no episode was captured.

detail.description: The attempt's own render-ready sentence, verbatim — 'drafted <kind> on <branch>', 'dispatched <command> for <phase>', 'asked N question(s) of <role>', or a failed venue's whole sentence including its run URL. comments.description: The anchored comments that rode with a send-back. note.description: The reviewer's send-back note, verbatim. Omitted unless outcome is sentBack and a note was recorded. On a persisted round it is the last send-back verdict's summary — the same words, read off the record that owns them instead of matched to it by position.

verdicts.description: Every reviewer's answer in this round, agent and human alike. Empty on a dispatch revision and on a revision reconstructed from a pre-ledger row.

thread.description: The round's comment thread with its replies and resolutions — the same comments the design rails' ArtifactSlot.reviewThread carries, which is a read-through to this until stage 6.

reviewers.description: The roster the round was opened with, as the reviewEngine computed it. Empty on a reconstructed revision: a pre-ledger row recorded who reviewed nowhere.

subjectRef.description: What this revision judged. The artifact as of a non-latest revision is read from it. Omitted on a reconstructed revision, which has no record of its subject.

decidedBy.description: Who decided the round. Omitted while it is undecided and on a reconstructed revision.

decidedAt.description: RFC3339, stamped by the store when the round was decided, verbatim. Omitted while it is undecided and on a reconstructed revision.

schema.description: The project.json document to judge (committed, or drafted at an artifact's gate).

designSessionAccess.notes: Design-slot mechanics only. A construction task's review lives on its activity's review round (StageTaskOutput, AppendReviewVerdict, SetReviewCommentStatus, DecideReviewRound); the artifact-kind-scoped send-back, comment-status and withdraw verbs that carried no activityId/taskId/roundId were deleted in dct4 (no caller after the co-author files' retirement). buildStatus.description: The component's build state: empty (the default — built or to be built), "planned" (designed, no code yet — derives no activity), or "external" (supplied outside the project). gitActivityStatusAccess.title: gitActivityStatusAccess contract

Ordinal 0 was Plan (N-STP) and 3 was SystemTest (N-IT) until 2026-10-02 (deterministic component testing, spec §7): neither is a testing variant again, and 3 is never reused.

gitActivityStatusAccess.notes: The git-forward PR/CI mirror, and nothing else. Variant.description: The testing variant of a testing activity; absent on every other row (the zero value is no variant, and ordinals 0 and 3 are retired).

Phase.description: The coarse lifecycle-phase roll-up. Meaningless when hasBuildEvidence is false (or classified is false): nothing has been resolved to roll up, so the value is the enum's zero, not a reported phase. Read it only when both flags are true.

recorded.description: True iff a stored .activityExecution head-state row exists for this activity. pendingResume.description: Present iff no construction pump opened this row (no start stamp) yet its attempt ledger resolves some lifecycle phases complete and others not: an integration-pending row the backfill recorded. When the pending notes exceed the 16 KiB one dispatch carries, the oldest wait for a later attempt so the newest arrives whole. A note recorded where no agent runs next (a merge-only retry, a takeover, or a finished activity) stays pending until the activity's next agent dispatch. Omitted when there are none.

id.description: The lifecycle phase's wire name: requirements, detailed_design, test_plan, construction or integration.

weight.description: The share of the activity's progress this lifecycle phase carries; the weights of one activity sum to 100.

completed.description: True iff the gate task's state is passed.
